claims.text: Introducing a gradient heterostructure can concurrently improve strength and ductility in metallic alloys.
Severe plastic deformation can create a controlled grain-size gradient.
High-pressure torsion or another severe-plastic-deformation method can produce a continuum from ultrafine surface grains to coarser interior grains.
The proposed processing conditions can generate the intended grain-size gradient during ambient-temperature deformation.
A grain-size gradient spatially varies local strength and ductility.
The gradient creates hetero-interfaces between harder fine-grained regions and more ductile coarse-grained regions.
A gradient microstructure promotes strain partitioning.
A gradient microstructure enhances the activation of multiple deformation mechanisms.
Fine-grained regions increase strength by blocking dislocation motion.
Coarser-grained regions provide a reservoir for plastic deformation.
The complementary behavior of fine- and coarse-grained regions synergistically improves ductility.
Compared with a uniformly processed sample, a gradient-structured material will have higher yield strength.
Compared with a uniformly processed sample, a gradient-structured material will have higher ultimate tensile strength.
Compared with a uniformly processed sample, a gradient-structured material will have greater uniform elongation before fracture.
The approach may be less effective when the contrast between soft and hard regions is insufficient.
The approach may require further tuning in materials already near their ductility limits.
The strength–ductility benefits may diminish if the grain-size gradient is too mild or overly steep.
Prior related studies support a general trend of improved strength–ductility balance through heterostructuring.
